description: Soil2Satellite is building a farmer-first app for Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. It compares a farm's current crop rotation with 2 better options using NASA POWER, SMAP & MODIS data, soil-card values and clear rules (no black box). I'm a full-stack dev (React/Next.js, Node/Express, Flask, Flutter, MongoDB). Looking for: UI/UX design, data viz, Earth science or agri knowledge, video/storytelling, and Kannada/Hindi speakers to test with farmers.
summary: Soil2Satellite is a web-based decision-support tool for the Field Shift challenge. It helps rainfed farmers and extension workers compare their current two-year crop rotation with evidence-backed alternatives before the next season is planted. A user drops a pin on their farm; the app retrieves 11 years (2015–2025) of daily NASA POWER climate data and NASA SRTM elevation, plus ISRIC SoilGrids soil estimates, and turns them into season-level indicators such as rainfall variability, dry spells and heat days. The user weights eight priorities, from water and nitrogen fixing to erosion, market and climate resilience. A deterministic engine screens every crop with seven feasibility checks, compares at least three strategies including the farmer's own, scores each transparently, tests whether the ranking holds when weights shift by ±10 points, and explains every option with its evidence, benefits, data gaps and local risks. Missing data stays missing; nothing is invented. This matters because rainfed farms carry the most climate risk: at our Tumakuru, Karnataka demo point, monsoon rainfall swung 3.6× between 2016 and 2022. Soil2Satellite turns free NASA data into an explained, shareable comparison a farmer can take to their local extension officer.
details:
What it does Soil2Satellite compares a farm's current crop rotation with evidence-backed alternatives over two years (Kharif, Rabi and Summer seasons). The farmer, or an extension worker on their behalf, sees which option best matches their own priorities, why, and what still needs checking locally.

How it works

  1. Locate the farm: search a village, use GPS or drop a pin; choose the water regime and the crops that can be sold locally.
  2. Retrieve evidence: the backend fetches 2015–2025 daily NASA POWER agroclimatology data (temperature, corrected precipitation, humidity, solar radiation), NASA SRTM elevation via OpenTopoData, and ISRIC SoilGrids soil properties.
  3. Build indicators: daily records become season-level rainfall, year-to-year variability (coefficient of variation), rainy days, longest dry spell, heat days above 35 °C, elevation and a slope proxy. Every value carries its source, resolution and limits; −999 fill values become "missing" and seasons need at least 50% daily coverage.
  4. Compare: the farmer enters their current rotation and weights eight priorities (water conservation, nitrogen fixing, erosion and soil cover, organic matter, forage, market suitability, operational feasibility, climate resilience). A deterministic engine generates alternatives from documented templates (legume break, bare-window cover crop, drought-hardy switch, diversification), runs seven feasibility checks per crop and season, scores each strategy, reports evidence coverage, and tests ranking sensitivity at ±10 weight points.
  5. Explain and export: each strategy has a five-part evidence card (why suggested, supporting evidence, potential benefits, information gaps, risks for local review) and the comparison downloads as PDF, CSV or JSON.

Benefits and intended impact The farmer's current practice is always the baseline, so advice starts from what they already do. Scores are transparent and explainable rather than a black-box prediction, and the tool never promises yield, profit or fertilizer doses. Extension workers (for example Krishi Vigyan Kendras) can run comparisons for many farms and hand farmers a PDF report. In the Tumakuru demo, a groundnut legume break scores 62.9 against 56.7 for the current ragi-then-fallow rotation, and the app shows exactly which priorities drive that difference.

Tools and languages Frontend: Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap, Recharts; static export hosted on Cloudflare. Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, httpx, fpdf2; Docker on AWS ECS Fargate. Data: NASA POWER Daily API, NASA SRTM (OpenTopoData), ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0, OpenStreetMap Nominatim. Crop requirements come from cited sources (FAO ECOCROP, FAO-56, ICAR, UAS-Bangalore, ICRISAT, SARE). Quality: 34 automated pytest tests plus an end-to-end smoke journey for both demo farms. No special hardware.

What makes it creative It compares whole multi-season rotations, including bare fallow windows, instead of recommending a single crop. It is provenance-first and honest: unavailable NASA layers (SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG, HLS NDVI) are listed in the app as data gaps, never faked, and mapped soil is always labelled "mapped estimate, not a soil test".

Factors we considered Spatial resolution (NASA POWER describes a ~50 km grid cell, not a field), missing data, farmer priorities that differ from farm to farm, explainability for non-experts, reliability during a live demo (24-hour cache and recorded real responses for demo farms), and the need for local expert review before any decision. Field validation with agronomists and farmers is the next step.

Use of SI tools Code was written with the help of AI coding assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Google Antigravity) and reviewed and tested by the developer. The presentation's layout, background art and charts were generated with AI assistance and are marked "SI-assisted" on every slide. The 30-second demo video's narration is AI-generated speech (Kokoro TTS), and its title cards, captions and music were AI-generated; the video carries a visible "SI-assisted" watermark and SI metadata. In the app, "Explain this comparison" can optionally use Google Gemini to reword the engine's structured result; a template is used otherwise. No data, indicators or scores are SI-generated: all come from the cited datasets and the deterministic engine.
